Turkey uses espionage accusations to pressure government critics

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1098 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, when police officers appeared at her home in Istanbul last Wednesday evening, Yonca Verdioglu Sik was surprised — even more so when they took her in for questioning.
  • But, according to transcripts of the interrogation that were published later, Verdioglu Sik was never asked any questions about espionage.
  • Sources indicate that for 18 years, Verdioglu Sik, who was born and raised in Germany, has been the foundation's project coordinator.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, when police officers appeared at her home in Istanbul last Wednesday evening, Yonca Verdioglu Sik was surprised — even more so when they took her in for questioning. Her lawyer states she was accused of political and military espionage.

But, according to transcripts of the interrogation that were published later, Verdioglu Sik was never asked any questions about espionage. Instead the public prosecutor's office appeared to be more interested in the activities of her German employer, the Heinrich Böll Foundation.

Sources indicate that for 18 years, Verdioglu Sik, who was born and raised in Germany, has been the foundation's project coordinator. In her role, she organizes projects that focus on democracy and the rights of women, minorities and LGBTQ+ people.

According to recent reports, during the interrogation, transfers of money from the foundation into her bank account were discussed. Verdioglu Sik found out that she was now also subject to a travel ban.

Verdioglu Sik was eventually released, but her arrest caused outrage among critics of the Turkish government. She is married to investigative journalist and member of parliament, Ahmet Sik. He belongs to the left-wing Workers' Party of Turkey, or TIP, and is known as one of the harshest critics of the current government.

Sik has recently been looking into a stock market scandal, which allegedly benefited members of the ruling Justice and Development Party, or AKP, headed by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, and associates.

Opposition critics drew a clear conclusion: As a member of parliament, Sik has parliamentary immunity. So instead, the justice system is putting pressure on him through his wife.

"If you take away a state's law, what is left is no longer called a state, but a gang," Sik responded to the arrest in writing.

Sources indicate that verdioglu Sik's arrest is not the first such case in Turkey. Ever since the attempted coup against the Erdogan government in 2016, accusations of espionage have been leveled at a wide variety of groups in Turkey: journalists, opposition figures and human rights activists as well as employees of foreign embassies and staff of foreign institutions like nongovernmental organizations and foundations.

In a recent development, such accusations have often been followed by acquittals or convictions for other offenses, albeit sometimes years later. But what the many instances have in common is what's known as a "chilling effect." Any investigation can mean lengthy pre-trial detention, reputational and professional damage and even social isolation.

In the past, such cases have even triggered diplomatic spats.

In 2015, for example, Can Dundar and Erdem Gul, both senior journalists at the opposition daily Cumhuriyet, were accused of espionage after reporting that Turkey had tried to ship arms to rebels fighting the Syrian government. Dundar now lives in exile in Berlin.

In 2017, Erdogan remarked that reporter Deniz Yücel, then working for German newspaper Die Welt, was a "German agent." That led to a serious diplomatic crisis between Berlin and Ankara.

Espionage charges have also been laid against local employees of the US diplomatic corps and against a lawyer working for the German embassy. US pastor Andrew Brunson and his wife were also arrested because of alleged links to Kurdish anti-government groups. Turkish philanthropist and human rights activist Osman Kavala, who was charged with espionage and attempting to overthrow the constitutional order, remains in prison.

Most recently, espionage charges have been brought against the former Istanbul mayor and Erdogan's political competitor, Ekrem Imamoglu, and a number of journalists.

Hakki Tas, a research fellow and expert on Turkey at the German Institute for Global and Area Studies, said the number of such cases have been increasing over the past few years.

Industry observers note that on the one hand, Turkey has the right to protect itself from foreign intelligence services — especially given geopolitical competition and conflict in the region, he argued. On the other hand, there's a long tradition of bringing the Turkish opposition to court to face security charges.

"What foreigners or employees of foreign institutions have experienced in recent years is a continuation of this pattern," Tas told DW.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Industry observers note that media outlets and NGOs critical of the government have faced investigations, trials and other sorts of state sanctions for years. The ruling AKP party has also brought in its own version of a so-called "foreign agent law.".

These sorts of espionage cases serve both a domestic and foreign policy function, Tas remarked.

In a recent development, for locals, "contact with a foreign institution, foreign funding or even a perfectly normal salary could become part of an investigation someday," he explained. "For opposition figures and civil society organizations, in particular, this can become a security concern.".

According to recent reports, in terms of foreign policy, the cases also show other countries that there are limits to their activities inside Turkey. These kinds of accusations seem to become more frequent when there's some sort of foreign policy tension — for example, after Western criticism of how opposition groups were dealt with after the alleged coup in 2016, the aforementioned disputes about arms deliveries in connection with Syria, or criticism from abroad about the removal of elected mayors in Turkey.

It can also serve as a kind of "hostage diplomacy," Tas said.

It has been revealed that the case of US pastor Brunson is a good example. After his arrest, the Turkish government proposed a trade with the Americans. They wanted to exchange Turkish preacher Fethullah Gulen, who lived in the US and who the Turkish government blamed for the 2016 coup attempt.

This suspicion of foreign institutions isn't something that the Erdogan government invented, Tas points out. In the early 2000s, several representatives of German organizations were already made to stand trial in Turkey. At the time, it was alleged that, among other things, the German spy service was using German foundations as a front for conspiracy.

In some of the best-known cases, defendants often don't end up convicted of espionage. In the case of activist Osman Kavala, he was initially acquitted of espionage several times and spent two years in prison, just because of those charges.

But Tas remarked that's no surprise, referring to a 1979 work about the sociology of law written by US law professor Malcolm Feeley. It's title: "The Process Is the Punishment.".

This article was originally written in German.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

David Moyes took a glug of water and glanced up at the substantial screen away to his right, almost as if he wanted confirmation that what he was seeing was true.

Sources indicate that had he looked behind him, Moyes would have seen Andy Burnham and his wife, Marie-France, in raptures, along with thousands of others. It was true, all right. Everton had scored their third goal and were bounding into the Carabao Cup quarter-finals, seemingly without a care in the world.

What a happy change of direction. Moyes has spent months spinning plates, dealing with owners who do not care about a proud club and want to sell up and a squad that was left criminally short in the transfer window. Then, before Newcastle’s visit, came more disruption.

Jack Grealish’s selfish and reckless decision to go Awol from training on Monday could have been a catalyst for more misery and invited Newcastle to deliver a hammer blow to Everton’s season, but again, Moyes fostered a siege mentality. He was rewarded in the most emphatic fashion.

True, Newcastle collapsed like a deckchair without hinges and this performance – which encouraged many of their 8,000 followers to head for the exits early – would not have done anything to convince those who view Matthias Jaissle, the head coach, with ambivalence to change their minds.

According to recent reports, the lack of discipline in their ranks was exposed when Dan Burn scored a late consolation and ended up in a melee with James Tarkowski and Joelinton. But the complications Jaissle, who lamented that “we must improve”, has to correct are for another day: this contest belonged to Everton.

Thierno Barry had provided the finish that secured a trip to Fleetwood in December and what an opportunity it is for Moyes to make Everton semi-finalists in this competition for the first time since 2016. Whether Grealish will have a part to play in it remains to be seen.

Thierno Barry with Everton's third! 🔵 https://t.co/dyb8fKud8N.

Sources indicate that the last thing Everton needed on a night of such importance was a distraction. Grealish will have a tough job mending relations, particularly with Moyes, but there was a paradox: though he had caused a major issue for 90 minutes he became an irrelevance.

Moyes is impatient to give Evertonians a significant day out and his only focus was on crossing this hurdle – for all that Newcastle have had a turbulent start to the campaign, they are dangerous opponents and you wondered in the fraught opening 30 minutes if they might exacerbate the hosts’ woes.

As Jaissle hopped and squirmed on the sidelines, imploring Newcastle forward, chances came and went: Harvey Barnes had a header saved, Fabian Schar tested Jordan Pickford from 30 yards while Vitalii Mykolenko and James Tarkowski made huge goal-saving challenges.

Industry observers note that “We should have scored more goals,” Jaissle, who was dressed as if auditioning for the role of The Milk Tray Man, growled. “It [losing] was shocking as the game was not that bad.”.

Moyes was infuriated by Everton’s initial inertia, so much so there was a point when the Scot prevented Merlin Röhl, his own full-back, from taking a throw-in until Tarkowski and Jake O’Brien had complied with his gesturing to get 10 yards further forward.

According to recent reports, it might have looked old-fashioned but it worked. Suddenly Everton started asking questions, Hayden Hackney almost got on the end of a cross from Mykolenko, and it encouraged the supporters on the vertiginous South Stand to raise their voices and become more involved.

What they needed was a goal to set things alight and in the 34th minute, it arrived. Tyrique George won possession by Newcastle’s corner flag, the ball dropped at Hackney’s feet and he instinctively ushered it on to James Garner, who whipped a right-footed drive beyond Lukáš Horníček.

In a recent development, james Garner puts Everton in front against Newcastle in the Carabao Cup! 🔵 https://t.co/TzponbWyGU.

Sources indicate that the roar that greeted it was a mix of elation and wonder, relief and desperation. The locals have grown weary of seeing nights with potential end in disappointment but here was the foothold they craved and the opportunity they were ready to seize. Soon the lead would be doubled.

Sources indicate that hackney would score the goal, converting a super Barry cross, but let us acknowledge the fabulous refereeing of Farai Hallam, who waved play on when he might have whistled for a foul on Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall. And how Everton took advantage.

Recent findings suggest that hayden Hackney doubles Everton's advantage! 🔵 https://t.co/VIY0Iln3nI.

It must be remarked the officiating this week has, in the main, been outstanding. Watching a match without the persistent spectre of VAR has been liberating and you can see the referees have felt free to make decisions on instinct.

According to recent reports, the whole experience of knowing a contest cannot be re-refereed has been better for all. It will not catch on, sadly, because too many people have gone too far down the road with VAR, but we should embrace the purity of “old school football” while we can.

Evertonians – the Prime Minister included – certainly embraced the buffer of a second goal and the fact Hackney scored it also felt like a throwback: a player who was plucked out of the Championship in the summer and encouraged by Moyes to show he could make the next step up.

Recent findings suggest that he did that and so, too, did Everton, their progress was assured in the 69th minute when Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall dashed down the left and crossed for Barry to finish. Moyes puffed out his cheeks as it hit the net. He, more than most, deserved to enjoy this one.

According to recent reports, the icy grip of relegation gets everyone in the end. Since William McGregor first came up with the idea of organised league football in 1888, every club to ever grace England's top flight has bowed out of the grand old competition.

It has been revealed that relegation is an all too recent memory for some sides, while others have gone more than 100 years without facing that bleak fate. Riches brought in by the advent of the Premier League in 1992 ensure that certain giants are practically impervious to the drop - as many as six clubs have contested every season. But history has proven that no team is safe.

For the first time since 1998, all three clubs that came up from the Championship were sent straight back down into the second tier at the end of the 2023/2024 campaign.

It has been revealed that that trend continued in the 2024/2025 Premier League season but came to an end when Leeds and Sunderland stayed up last term. Below is a look at when every Premier League team was last relegated.

According to recent reports, the Tractor Boys are back in the top flight after one season in the Championship. Kieran McKenna guided Ipswich Town into the Premier League for the first time in over 20 years in 2024, but they were instantly relegated in the 2024/25 season.

Sources indicate that however, they bounced straight back into the automatic play-off places. Gary O'Neil is the man in charge at Portman Road, and he'll be hoping to improve on McKenna's 19th-place finish with just 22 points.

Leeds United's relegation to the Championship was confirmed following a heavy 4-1 defeat against Tottenham Hotspur on the final day of the Premier League campaign at Elland Road.

It was a result which summed up their season as they went into the clash with Spurs knowing they needed to win, before conceding two minutes into the game and then two minutes into the second half.

Leeds conceded a league-high 78 goals across the season, while manager Sam Allardyce described his side's finishing as "inept" on the final day.

Industry observers note that relegation was a depressingly familiar sensation for Fulham fans by the summer of 2021 as the west London outfit fell out of England's top flight for the third time in seven years. Former club captain Scott Parker was at the helm throughout a campaign short on excitement.

According to recent reports, bobby Decordova-Reid mustered a team-high five goals, the lowest tally of any top scorer in the club's history. Parker was adamant that Fulham would avoid relegation right up until it became a mathematical certainty, railing against the majority who may have thought that he was "living in cuckoo land". His confidence was misplaced.

Eddie Howe took over as Bournemouth boss in 2008 when the club was inside League Two's relegation zone. The Cherries avoided the drop despite a 17-point deduction and spent five seasons in the Premier League before going through the trap door.

Bournemouth were still under Howe's stewardship when they fell one point short of safety in 2020, tumbling into the Championship despite defeating an Everton side which finished in mid-table on the final day. The south coast outfit conceded at least 60 goals in each top-flight campaign under Howe and injuries to their forward line that season robbed them of the firepower which had offered salvation in the past.

Hull City's last Premier League campaign in a decade came in 2016/17. A team with some notable names, such as Harry Maguire and Andy Robertson, were demoted to the second tier on May 14 after a 4-0 defeat at Crystal Palace.

Sources indicate that the Tigers ended up seven points from safety after the 38th match, having conceded 80 goals, more than any other Premier League side that season. They're back where they want to be, and will be aiming to secure safety in 2026-27.

Sunderland's 10-year stay in the Premier League ended with four matches of the season left to play as Bournemouth came to the Stadium of Light and secured a 1-0 win.

The result against the Cherries was the Black Cats' 23rd defeat of a poor campaign in which they didn't win their first until November, and they would go on to record three more losses in their final four games.

Sunderland's blank against Bournemouth was their 18th in 34 matches, with their lack of ruthlessness one of the reasons why they finally lost their Premier League status in David Moyes' first season in charge.

Recent findings suggest that there have been few bleaker days in the history of Newcastle United than 11th May 2016. The club's fierce local rivals Sunderland, who were led by former Newcastle boss Sam Allardyce, earned a commanding victory over Everton to send the Magpies into the Championship.

According to recent reports, A buoyant crowd at the Stadium of Light bellowed: "Are you watching Newcastle?" Only those with a penchant for punishment were still tuning in to see Lamine Kone lash Sunderland into a 3-0 lead. Their fate may have been confirmed by the final day of the season, but Newcastle romped to a 5-1 win against a Tottenham team that had spent most of the campaign fighting for the title.

Industry observers note that aston Villa finished the 2015/16 campaign with more managers (four) than victories (three). Remi Garde was the third forlorn figure through the door by November and lost the dressing room immediately. Former Premier League winner Micah Richards described Garde's first set of drills as "pathetic" and "under-8s football".

"So from that moment in the training session, we knew full well that we were going down," Richards revealed. The French coach was in charge of a 6-0 thrashing at home to Liverpool, which began a sequence of 11 consecutive defeats. Garde and his children's games were gone before Villa stopped the rot.

In a recent development, crystal Palace needed to defeat Charlton Athletic on the final day of the 2004/2005 season to avoid relegation. The Eagles were 2-1 up with eight minutes left when Jerome Thomas swung a free-kick into the box.

Sources indicate that palace boss Iain Dowie plastered posters which read: "How much do I want it?" around the club's training ground heading into the final months of the season. Goalkeeper Gabor Kiraly wanted it less than Charlton's Jonathan Fortune, jumping under the ball as the defender headed the hosts level. Dowie looked on dumbfounded - perhaps he should have provided an answer to his rhetorical question - as Palace sank into the second tier.

Joe Royle didn't have the strength to muster a rousing speech after his Manchester City side were consigned to relegation in 2001, exactly one year after winning promotion to the Premier League. Asked about next season, Royle countered: "Let's all be miserable for a while first.".

In a recent development, in the years before Manchester City were taken over by some of the richest owners in English football, the Sky Blues bounced freely between the various tiers of the football pyramid. Royle oversaw two relegations and as many promotions in less than four years at the helm. City's focus is fixed firmly at the opposite end of the table these days.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Paul Merson has claimed that Liverpool were happy enough to allow Xabi Alonso to take the Chelsea manager’s job earlier this year after Arne Slot was dismissed.

Having spent five years with the Reds during his playing career, the former Spain midfielder was widely touted to return to Anfield in a managerial capacity as speculation grew over the Dutchman’s future before he was eventually dismissed in May.

However, the 44-year-old was appointed at Stamford Bridge instead, replacing Liam Rosenior as permanent boss following Calum McFarlane’s caretaker spell at the end of last season.

Hopes of a Champions League finish and maybe even a tilt at a title challenge have since been extinguished by five defeats from Chelsea’s first 11 Premier League games under Alonso, the latest of which was a 4-1 home thrashing by Leeds on Saturday.

Want more CaughtOffside coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust.

In a recent development, merson feels that Liverpool suspected their former player wasn’t up to the task of replacing Slot in the summer, writing in his Sky Sports column: ‘My biggest worry is that Liverpool could have had Xabi Alonso and they chose not to. Obviously, Liverpool didn’t think he was good enough.

‘Alonso took the Chelsea job and Liverpool sacked Arne Slot two weeks later. You can’t tell me that Liverpool couldn’t have spoken to Alonso and say: ‘Don’t take the Chelsea job; we’re going to take you’.

In a recent development, ‘He was out of a job as well, Liverpool could have had him and he’d have gone there all day long, so why didn’t they take him? Did they know something that we’re seeing now? It just always sits in my mind. That was my worry – and now it’s playing out.

‘If this was Liam Rosenior in charge at Chelsea and getting these results, he’d be in major trouble. 100%, he’d be in trouble. Remember, Rosenior didn’t have Morgan Rogers in his Chelsea team, bought for £116m, but it’s because of the unbelievable job [Alonso] did at Bayer Leverkusen that everybody is thinking: ‘It will be alright’.’.

The Stamford Bridge hierarchy aren’t known for their patience with managers/head coaches, with Alonso the sixth permanent Chelsea boss in this decade alone, and reports that the club are considering a move for Cesc Fabregas in the future won’t have helped his case.

The Daily Mail reported in the wake of the Leeds thrashing that the 44-year-old is in no imminent danger of losing his job just yet, with Blues chiefs conscious of how the tactician overcame an inconsistent start at Bayer Leverkusen to win an unbeaten domestic double in 2023/24.

There’s no escaping the truth that Chelsea have had a disappointing campaign so far, with as many defeats as wins in the Premier League and, despite having no European football, bowing out of the Carabao Cup after losing to Liverpool on penalties last month.

It’s not the start to life in west London that Alonso would’ve envisaged, but any suggestions that he should face the sack this early into his tenure are nonsensical.

In a recent development, at the very least, he deserves the full campaign to try and achieve the Blues pre-season aims, unless their form were to plummet to Manchester United levels in the meantime. With that being unlikely, patience is a virtue that Stamford Bridge chiefs ought to exercise.

Wolf Biermann at 90: The singer who defied East Germany

💡 Key Takeaways
  • He mocks Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin as "political lovers," denounces the "endless fratricidal war" over the Palestinian territories, and repeatedly invokes "Lady Liberty." It is a celebration of the freedom he once so painfully lacked in the former East Germany, and of the freedom people around the world still yearn for.
  • In a recent development, these themes run throughout Wolf Biermann's fresh album "Unterm Haar nur Himmel" ("Beneath Hair, Only Sky") released to mark his 90th birthday.
  • Biermann remains one of Germany's most influential singer-songwriters, and at 90, he shows little sign of putting down his guitar.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

He mocks Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin as "political lovers," denounces the "endless fratricidal war" over the Palestinian territories, and repeatedly invokes "Lady Liberty." It is a celebration of the freedom he once so painfully lacked in the former East Germany, and of the freedom people around the world still yearn for.

In a recent development, these themes run throughout Wolf Biermann's fresh album "Unterm Haar nur Himmel" ("Beneath Hair, Only Sky") released to mark his 90th birthday. The album's title is a characteristically poetic phrase coined by Biermann himself. It evokes the idea that however restrictive the world may become, the human mind and spirit remain free. Beneath the hair lies open sky: a metaphor for inner freedom, independence and imagination.

Biermann remains one of Germany's most influential singer-songwriters, and at 90, he shows little sign of putting down his guitar. Often described as Germany's answer to Bob Dylan, the outspoken troubadour continues to weigh in on the concerns shaping the world today.

In his recent song "Moritat von den Liebespaaren" ("Ballad of the Lovers"), he delivers a simple but urgent message: no single person can save the world, yet everyone can help make it a better place. Above all, the song is a call to take responsibility for one's own life rather than remain a bystander.

Industry observers note that this outspokenness was instilled in Biermann early on. When he was born in Hamburg in 1936, Adolf Hitler was already in power. His father was a dockworker, a committed communist, a resistance fighter against the Nazis — and Jewish.

Wolf was just three months old when the Gestapo, Hitler's secret police, arrested his father. He initially served time in prison before he was murdered by the Nazis at Auschwitz in early 1943.

Just a few months later, British and American bombers attacked Hamburg, unleashing a devastating firestorm. "Nothing in my life has shaped me more," Biermann has repeatedly said in interviews. When the sirens sounded, his mother took him into an air raid shelter. The house above them was burning.

Yet Biermann has stated his memories of that time are rooted in a profound sense of trust in life. In an interview with the German magazine Chrismon, he recalled: "I pressed my face into my mother's soft coat so I could breathe. A sense of security in the midst of the end of the world. We stumbled out over the neighboring house and into the open. The firestorm lifted a burning roof into the air. Roaring corrugated metal, smoke everywhere. We searched for a way out. [...] Death was everywhere. 40,000 people died. They had no chance. But I did. My strong mama.".

Industry observers note that biermann's mother instilled communist and anti-fascist ideas in him with almost religious fervor. "My mother had only one goal after those dark years," Biermann once recalled. "I was supposed to survive so that I could, as she put it rather grandly, one day take revenge for my father's death. I was supposed to build communism.".

In 1953, while countless people were fleeing East Germany, Biermann moved there of his own free will — after all, communism was the official state ideology. He was just 16 at the time. In East Berlin, he studied political economy, mathematics and philosophy. His role models were writers Bertolt Brecht and Heinrich Heine. He began working as an assistant director at the Berliner Ensemble, and also began writing and performing his political songs.

Biermann soon realized that life in East Germany was far from the communist paradise he had imagined and he wrote about this openly in his songs. "The party bosses were torn," Biermann noted. "They were delighted by this young poet who could play the guitar so beautifully and sing such cheeky songs. They thought they just needed to bring me into line. Even today, I'm amazed that I wound up cast in the role of the heroic dragon slayer.".

Industry observers note that in 1965, East Germany's ruling Socialist Unity Party, the SED, imposed a blanket ban on Biermann performing or publishing his work. His East Berlin apartment, which was under constant surveillance, soon became a gathering place for dissidents and critical thinkers.

In a recent development, yet, to his great surprise, the East German authorities allowed him to travel to Cologne, West Germany in 1976. There, around 7,000 people flocked to see him. For four and a half hours, he strummed and sang, mocking the East German regime. His songs were so popular that bootleg copies found their way back to East Germany.

Sources indicate that on November 16, while still on tour in West Germany, Biermann heard the news on his car radio that he had been stripped of his right to continue residing in the German Democratic Republic. The regime accused him of betraying and slandering East Germany. ".

I felt like the ground had opened up beneath me. I was overcome with fear, everything went dark," Biermann wrote in his memoirs.

It has been revealed that in a petition, leading East German intellectuals spoke out against the decision. In response, the regime stepped up surveillance of dissidents, imposed professional bans and jailed its critics. Several prominent public figures left the country.

Sources indicate that "The SED leadership expected an angry media response from the West. What they hadn't reckoned with was that, for the very first time, a group of respected East German writers and artists would make their protest public, disguising it as a humble petition," Biermann wrote.

According to recent reports, afterward, Biermann sank into a deep depression. "Not just because I had been torn away from the friends I knew and loved in East Berlin, but also because I had lost my familiar mortal enemies," he said.

It has been revealed that he became involved in the peace and anti-nuclear movements and continued singing about the injustices of the world. "The world's conflicts take different forms in each generation," he said. "But it's always the same struggle for freedom.".

It has been revealed that the singer-songwriter prepares to spend his 90th birthday at home in Hamburg with his wife and manager, Pamela. For the first time in his life, he stated, he's skipping the birthday party, even with his 10 children.

"I'm so old and I can feel my strength fading. And I know that the next day I have a major concert at the Berliner Ensemble," he told the German Press Agency.

And should he ever die, he said, he wants to be buried at Berlin's cemetery where some renowned German writers and intellectuals have been laid to rest, among them Bertolt Brecht, Anna Seghers and Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel. He still has a thing or two to discuss with them.

This article was originally written in German.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

So where do Manchester United go from here? It is never a good look when opposition fans start willing a rival club to stick with their manager, but that was the ignominy that had befallen Michael Carrick by the end of an afternoon in which Lisandro Martinez’s latest plastic hardman impression embodied the very worst of United’s self-sabotage.

After seeing their team go 2-0 up when Cole Palmer converted the penalty given away by Martinez’s lunacy, the Chelsea fans taunted Carrick with chants of “You’re getting sacked in the morning” and later “You’re going down with the City”, a nod to the other Manchester club who are crisis torn for very different reasons.

As the final whistle loomed, though, and with United just grateful Estevao had not punished Martinez’s red card more severely, the Chelsea fans had changed their tune. “Michael Carrick, we want you to stay,” came the chant from the Matthew Harding Stand and that cut far deeper.

And to think that the opening 45 minutes had offered United and their fans some hope of a little respite from the storm before ultimately giving way to an ever-darkening gloom.

According to recent reports, carrick, who had been given a stay of execution in midweek, said he still expected to be in charge for Roma’s visit to Old Trafford on Tuesday in the Champions League. But it is hard to escape the feeling that another managerial change will be coming at United before too long even if no one can be sure what happens next.

Equally, the prospect of more upheaval in the dugout might elicit little more than a shrug from fans pointing the finger squarely at the ownership and the executives they have appointed. The players were spared this time but Sir Jim Ratcliffe and the Glazers remained the target of sustained abuse as did Jason Wilcox, the director of football.

Defeat here extended United’s winless run to nine matches, their worst sequence for 38 years. They have taken just four points from the last 21 on offer in the Premier League and seem to be sinking fast. Carrick was asked about the team becoming mired in a relegation battle. This is the territory United are in.

The strange thing is this could and probably should have been a day when they at least stopped the rot for a few days. But more non-existent defending and brainlessness from Martinez, who was sent off for planting an elbow in Wesley Fofana’s face, put paid to that in a second half in which Carrick admitted United “unravelled”.

Chelsea were cut open on at least five occasions in a see-saw first half and Matheus Cunha also had a goal disallowed for a narrow offside. Xabi Alonso’s side had opportunities of their own – you will always get them against this United team – but they were second best and lucky not to be behind. Everyone talks about United being there for the taking, but the truth is Chelsea, coming off the back of a miserable defeat to Spurs and Carabao Cup exit to Liverpool, were here.

Recent findings suggest that the problem is Carrick’s team could not hit a barn door at the moment. They have scored just three goals in their last six league games and that lack of cutting edge was evident in the way Bruno Fernandes, back in the team as captain, and Amad Diallo (dangerous but with no end product) wasted excellent chances. That wastefulness would put pressure on any back line, let alone one with all the fortitude of wet cardboard. Chelsea were spared and exploited it with the help of the second and most corrosive acts of United’s self-mutilation.

We will come to Martinez’s sending off in a moment, but there had already been a cowardly act of a different kind from the Argentine defender before then in the lead-up to Chelsea’s opening goal soon after the restart.

Take nothing away from Morgan Rogers – his 40yd dash from the edge of the centre circle in United’s half to the six-yard box and the finish that followed were top notch. But where was the challenge? How could not a single player in red have stood in his path? “Come on Morgan, run through us buddy” seemed to be the message.

Good morning and welcome to live coverage of the Premier League match between Chelsea, who start the day in fifth, and 16th-placed Manchester United at Stamford Bridge. On Sunday and Monday it seemed certain that Michael Carrick would be relieved of his duties before today’s game but has survived for now, hoping to turn things around in the no man’s land that sometimes resembles a vote of confidence and at others a stay of execution.

Thirty years ago when Newcastle United were coming off the bridle in the title race with Manchester United, Alex Ferguson, as he then was, accused a Leeds team, who had been in freefall since the fresh year, of professional malpractice when they put in a rare display of passionate commitment and tenacity at Old Trafford in a 1-0 defeat.

It has been revealed that “Why are they not in the top six?” asked Ferguson. “To me they’re cheating their manager. You wait and see the difference when they play Newcastle.” The hate between the Leeds and Manchester united fanbases was such, he implied, that they had decided to put a shift in because, for once, they feared the consequences if they had not. It seems to this observer that the boot is now on the other foot. These Manchester United players roused themselves to fight at Elland Road then chucked it in against Como and Bournemouth. If that’s not “cheating their manager”, what is?

Carrick will have to hope that some of the old hostility between Chelsea and Manchester United might encourage the players to run about a bit this afternoon and, at the very least, get stuck in rather than crumple spinelessly as they did last week. I doubt it would be enough to save Carrick’s job in the medium term but at least it would address whether they could stake a claim to be part of the rebuilding process.

Industry observers note that as for Chelsea, who were awful in defeat by Brentford and Spurs either side of impressive victories over Bournemouth and at Everton, they need to find some defensive solidity, discipline and a way of terrorising defences in the absence of Joao Pedro. They are a work in progress still, in the fifth year of the hedge fund hegemony. For all that attacking talent and Moises Caicedo’s ability to steamroll midfielders, their defence does not inspire confidence and last year’s petulance continues to simmer.

Newcastle United are among several Premier League clubs interested in signing Lazio midfielder Kenneth Taylor, with competition for the Dutch international expected to intensify ahead of the January transfer window.

The Magpies are looking to strengthen their midfield options, and the 24-year-old has emerged as a potential target following his impressive performances in Italy. However, they face competition from Brentford, Bournemouth and Juventus, who are also watching his situation closely.

Recent findings suggest that according to a TEAMtalk report, Taylor has attracted considerable interest after establishing himself as an important player at Lazio. The midfielder has adapted well to Italian football since joining from Ajax earlier this year, and his consistent performances have made him an attractive option for several clubs.

Taylor could be an excellent addition to Newcastle’s midfield. His ability to dictate the tempo, carry the ball forward and contribute in the final third would offer Eddie Howe greater flexibility in his squad. The Dutchman has already registered five goals and four assists in 33 appearances for Lazio, showing he can influence matches at both ends of the pitch.

Juventus are reportedly leading the pursuit of the midfielder and are considering a proposal worth approximately €40 million to secure his services. Newcastle, Brentford and Bournemouth are also interested, with the latter potentially looking for replacements should Alex Scott leave.

According to recent reports, however, a January transfer could prove difficult to negotiate. Lazio are reluctant to lose key players mid-season, particularly given their strong position in Serie A.

Taylor is also contracted until 2030, leaving the Italian club in a strong position to demand a substantial transfer fee.

Newcastle will need to explore alternative options if Lazio refuse to negotiate in January, although Taylor could remain an attractive target for the summer transfer window.

These gaps in weather data affect forecasts everywhere: plugging them is not charity

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (992 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that observations from data-scarce regions, such as low-lying island Tuvalu in the South Pacific, are crucial to weather forecasts, early warning systems and climate-information services elsewhere.
  • Sources indicate that when I talk about collecting essential weather and climate data in countries with limited resources, many take it to mean that wealthier countries, institutions and firms should ‘help poorer ones’.
  • That’s the resounding conclusion of a report published this month by The European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) in collaboration with the World Meteorological Organization (WMO).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that observations from data-scarce regions, such as low-lying island Tuvalu in the South Pacific, are crucial to weather forecasts, early warning systems and climate-information services elsewhere. Credit: Mario Tama/Getty.

Sources indicate that when I talk about collecting essential weather and climate data in countries with limited resources, many take it to mean that wealthier countries, institutions and firms should ‘help poorer ones’. But as a development and climate-finance executive, I know that this is an investment rather than an act of charity. Science proves it: better forecasts at home rely on observations abroad.

That’s the resounding conclusion of a report published this month by The European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) in collaboration with the World Meteorological Organization (WMO). The report was commissioned by the Systematic Observations Financing Facility (SOFF), a United Nations fund dedicated to basic weather and climate data around the world, of which I am a director.

Its aim was to establish the benefits of filling gaps in the WMO’s Global Basic Observing Network (GBON), which defines member nations’ mandatory weather-station coverage. To comply, each country must have a land station every 200 kilometres, as well as a weather balloon every 500 kilometres over land and every 1,000 kilometres over sea to collect data on essential variables (such as temperature, pressure, humidity and wind).

Global climate body fights for survival: why the IPCC must be saved.

Global climate body fights for survival: why the IPCC must be saved.

But agreeing on standards and sites is not the same as having the economic means to implement them. Since 2023, GBON stations have been required to share their data. Yet, about 90% of weather data from low-income countries and small island nations are not being shared. Some data are not even collected because many stations are missing, stopped working or cannot transmit their measurements.

It has been revealed that these gaps don’t just impede local forecasts, they affect regional and global projections too. Daily weather data feed into increasingly sophisticated computer models that predict how weather systems around the world evolve.

Think of a weather forecast as a photograph. It is made up of millions of pixels, each contributing a small piece of information. Weather forecasting is more complex, but the analogy helps to explain the problem: if too many ‘pixels’ are missing, the global picture is blurry or incomplete. And for forecasts, some ‘pixels’, or observations, are more valuable than others. Plugging gaps in data-scarce regions is the best way to improve forecasts everywhere.

It is also a matter of justice: on average, a seven-day temperature forecast in a high-income country is as accurate as a one-day forecast in a low-income country (M. Linsenmeier and J. G. Shrader Nature Commun. 17, 10792; 2026).

According to recent reports, the results of the ECMWF simulations are striking. Better coverage in low-income countries and small island states can cut uncertainty in 12-hour local forecasts by more than 30% in parts of Africa and by up to 20% across the Pacific.

According to recent reports, extra data in all countries eligible for development assistance and small island nations would improve the accuracy of temperature and wind forecasts up to six or seven days ahead in the tropics, home to some 40% of the world’s population, and in the Northern Hemisphere’s mid-latitudes, where much of Europe, North America and northern Asia sit. This would help with, for example, aviation and maritime operations, planning of agricultural activities, water management and preparations for severe weather.

Industry observers note that disparity in countries’ capacity to finance weather observations is striking. To quantify the inequality, SOFF developed an indicator comparing countries’ gross dom-estic product (GDP) with the geographical area for which they are mandated to provide observations, including marine exclusive economic zones. For example, although it is a small country, Switzerland has a larger budget than does Tuvalu, a Pacific island nation spread across an immense ocean area (Switzerland’s GDP is around 300,000 times larger per square kilometre). Yet both countries contribute to and benefit from the same global observing system.

By CALUM CROWE, SCOTTISH DEPUTY CHIEF SPORTS WRITER.

Published: 10:52 EST, 23 November 2026 | Updated: 11:15 EST, 23 November 2026.

Rangers boss Derek McInnes insists the incentive of next month's Premier Sports Cup Final can fuel his players as they prepare to embark on a vital run of fixtures.

A 2-1 triumph over Motherwell on Saturday night stretched Rangers' unbeaten run to 13 matches after Ryan Naderi struck a late winner at Fir Park.

McInnes' side will host a revitalised Aberdeen at Ibrox on Tuesday night, before two further home matches against Falkirk and Dundee United over the next week.

They will then face a double-header against Hibs, with a league clash at Easter Road swiftly followed by the cup final.

McInnes insists no player is guaranteed their place in the team - and challenged them to earn their place for the Hampden showpiece as they look to win the first trophy of the season.

'I think the squad looks strong at the minute,' said the Ibrox boss. 'We've got good options and good options from the bench to turn to.

Derek McInnes has led Rangers on a 13-game unbeaten run in all competitions.

'In this little run of fixtures, hopefully everybody will start to play a wee bit more of their part and hopefully more winning performances.

'I don't think I'll mention it [the cup final] too often, but they are not daft, they see that and everybody wants to play in the team.

'Anybody who's in the team needs to keep playing well to stay in the team and anybody who's not in the team needs to train right and take advantage of their minutes.

According to recent reports, 'We make that point often enough. Sometimes you've got to go away to tough venues like Motherwell and do the hard work and get the reward.

'But there's bigger games, more games like cup finals to take part in, so everybody wants to play in that one.

'I'm sure it does us no harm. I think it keeps the fans bubbling along, a chance of silverware, so when it comes along hopefully, as I say, we're in good form.'.

Rangers are on a strong run of form and haven't lost a game since they were dumped out of Europe against Jablonec at the end of August.

The victory over Motherwell maintained their position in second in the table, four points adrift of Celtic with a game in hand.

Up against an Aberdeen side buoyed by their first win under upcoming boss Mario Frick at the weekend, McInnes wants his players to keep the pedal to the metal.

'I think it's unusual with five games now away from Ibrox, four in the league and the cup game, and now the fixtures kind of run the other way,' noted the Rangers boss.

'We've got some good fixtures at home but I think we always look at little blocks in the weeks, and where we're looking to try and get to by a certain period, and get certain points and certain targets.

According to recent reports, 'But first thing's first now with Aberdeen. We've got to make sure we're a strong home team again. Hopefully we can score a few more goals but, ultimately, as long as we win the game, I'll be happy.

'I think there's always a wee concern when you've got so many away on an international break, but obviously now with the January break gone, this is us working right through to March.

'When you look at those little blocks of games, and where the teams are, it's important that we just put our shoulder to the wheel.

'Every game is going to bring up different challenges and just because we're at Ibrox, it's an advantage, but it doesn't guarantee anything. We've got to use that advantage properly.

'As I say, we've got some fixtures now ahead of the cup final. Hopefully we can get into the cup final in good form and with some strong performances.'.

Venezuelan striker Kevin Kelsy could be in line to start against Aberdeen.

Kevin Kelsy could be in line for a bigger role this week after fatigue caused by his return from international duty limited his involvement in Saturday's win over Motherwell.

The Venezuela striker was only fit enough for a substitute appearance after enduring a gruelling journey back from a friendly in Russia, with Derek McInnes admitting the travel disruption had taken its toll.

'When you go away on international duty, they go to some far-flung places and playing a friendly in Russia is not the best preparation,' said the Rangers boss.

Industry observers note that 'There was a point on Thursday morning when we were really worried about whether he was getting back. To have ten-and-a-half hours in an airport all day Thursday isn't ideal preparation.

'He was gubbed on Friday. He was very tired when he spoke to me and told me he hadn't really slept.

'It's been a bit unusual, the preparation. We sent him home early on Friday to get a good sleep and look after himself, but we just made the call we thought was the right thing to do.

'We needed everybody at it on Saturday and we've got a massive week ahead of us where he can play his part, hopefully from the start in one or two of these games.'.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that spain won 2-0 in Prague despite missing Lamine Yamal, Rodri and Mikel Oyarzabal, with Atlético Madrid's Álex Baena converting a penalty and Marc Pubill adding a late second. The win keeps the world champions perfect in Nations League Group A3 and leaves them needing only a draw against England on Sunday.

Spain beat ten-man Czechia 2-0 at the Letná Stadium in Prague on Thursday. They did it without three of their leading names. Lamine Yamal, Rodri and Mikel Oyarzabal were all missing. Atlético Madrid’s Álex Baena struck from the spot, and Marc Pubill added a late second. The world champions remain perfect in Group A3 before Sunday’s decider against England.

Conditions were raw. The game was played in 4°C, with light drizzle and humidity above 90%, the Spanish federation mentioned. Czechia are coached by the Spaniard Santi Denia.

Industry observers note that chances were scarce before the break. Dean Huijsen’s header was Spain’s only open-play effort on target in the first half, and it was easily saved. The breakthrough came from the penalty spot. Lukáš Ambros was penalised for handball in the area. Baena’s powerful penalty beat goalkeeper Matěj Kovář.

Spain thought they had doubled the lead after half-time. VAR ruled out an effort by Yéremy Pino. The game was physical. Referee Nikola Dabanovic booked Pedro Porro in the 12th minute and Mikel Merino in the 69th. He then dismissed Krejčí, leaving the hosts a man down for the closing stages.

Spain made the extra man count deep into added time. Pubill won the ball back in Czechia’s half and rolled it into the bottom corner. That settled the contest. For Atlético followers, Baena’s goal was the night’s highlight. Fermín López, by contrast, is still waiting for his first Spain goal.

Recent findings suggest that the victory was Spain’s 12th in a row and their fifth straight win in the Nations League. ESPN mentioned it stretched their record unbeaten run in all competitions. Spain’s last defeat came against Colombia in March 2024. Czechia, meanwhile, have lost every Nations League game this season.

It has been revealed that england kept pace on the same night. They beat Croatia 2-1 at Wembley and sit three points behind Spain. That sets up a straight shoot-out for first place. A draw against England at the Metropolitano on Sunday will be enough for Spain to finish first in the group.

There were a few suggestions that the Englishman could potentially be available for the trip to Anfield, but it appears as though it could now take a few games longer.

What is clear is that Pochettino will be desperate to have Shaw back in the starting XI as soon as possible, having loved working with him during the duo's time together at Southampton.

Como coach Cesc Fabregas claims he’ll take the same approach as Frosinone coach Massimiliano Alvini for the upcoming Champions League match against AEK Athens: ‘I’m sticking to my ideas.’.

Como are preparing for a home Champions League game against AEK Athens, and Fabregas spoke at a press conference on Monday, the eve of the game.

Como are the best-placed Serie A club in the Champions League so far as they sit fourth with nine points in four matches.

They’ve won seven of their last eight games across all competitions, including a 9-1 win over Lens in the previous Champions League round.

Fabregas remarked he wouldn’t change the team’s identity for their upcoming European match, citing Frosinone coach Alvini the day after a 5-1 loss to Milan.

Industry observers note that “I’m taking the same approach as Alvini against Milan. I’m sticking to my ideas,” Fabregas remarked via Gazzetta.

It has been revealed that “Of course, there are games we need to know how to manage in order to win, but we’re not going to change all the good things we’re doing. I’m proud of our last match against Cagliari, which featured so many new elements: players returning from international duty, Da Cunha playing as a No.10 instead of Paz, a role he hasn’t played in very often.

Recent findings suggest that “Then Ricci and Liberali started and did well, and Lahdo made a positive impact off the bench. All of that tells you the team is there, that they understand what they want to do and how to do it. I like stability and being able to control everything, even if it’s difficult.”.

Frosinone remain the most surprising team in Serie A as the newly-promoted Serie A side sit seventh and even beat Como 2-0 in September.

Against Milan, they refused to sit deep and remained true to their identity, but ultimately conceded five goals on the counter away at San Siro.

“Today, I still want to hear people say Alvini is a great coach. That is identity and courage, even if he lost 5-1,” Fabregas insisted.

“When you lose, you’re rubbish; when you win, you’re a genius. You need to keep things in perspective. Football is certainly changing, partly because referees are blowing their whistles less. Fewer players are staying down because that tactic no longer works. It’s a positive turning point for the Italian league, which is becoming one of the two or three most entertaining in Europe.”.

Como have already beaten RB Leipzig, Manchester United and Lille in the Champions League, and tomorrow they’ll be the favourite side against AEK.

“Nothing changes for us. We’re a small club that knows exactly who we are,” Fabregas said.

“There’s a fantastic atmosphere at Mozzate. We know our strengths and weaknesses. We can’t control what people say; we have to be stronger and manage our emotions. The players are getting a lot more attention, and that helps them mature, too. If they want to reach the top, they have to know how to handle that too. We’re still right at the beginning. We’re focusing on the journey, not the destination.

In a recent development, “AEK are a great team. They caused problems for Real and Shakhtar; they’re physically strong and have a great mentality. We’ll need to be very clinical.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At a time when press freedom is under pressure and international newsrooms are shrinking, the Werner Holzer Prize celebrates a profession that many consider indispensable to democracy: foreign correspondence.

In a recent development, presented in honor of Werner Holzer, the veteran reporter and former editor-in-chief of the German daily newspaper Frankfurter Rundschau, this year's award coincided with what would have been his 100th birthday. Holzer spent decades reporting from some of the world's most important hot spots and championing international journalism.

At the award ceremony in Frankfurt's Römer, the city's historic town hall, Mayor Mike Josef recalled that fundamental rights such as freedom of speech and freedom of the press were first enshrined for all Germans by the Frankfurt Parliament in the nearby Paulskirche in 1848.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

In a recent development, the 2026 winners reflect the breadth and ambition of the award. First prize went to Katja Gloger, a veteran Russia correspondent who moved to Moscow in 1989 and accompanied Vladimir Putin during the early years of his presidency.

In her recent nonfiction book, "The Failure: An Investigative Report of Germany's Russia Policy," Gloger and co-author Georg Mascolo offer a searing critique of the misjudgments and illusions that shaped German policy toward Russia for decades.

Second prize was awarded to DW journalist and presenter Jaafar Abdul Karim. His talk show JaafarTalk reaches millions of viewers across the Arab world and in Germany. Whether in Tunis, Beirut or Cairo, Abdul Karim tackles subjects that are often considered taboo.

A research grant went to freelance journalist Luise Land, whose current project explores why her German-Namibian family still owns extensive landholdings in Namibia today. By tracing that history, she examines the enduring legacy of the genocide against the Herero and Nama peoples by German colonial forces in the early 20th century.

"Katja Gloger is one of the leading foreign policy reporters. For decades, she has been among the foremost experts on Russia and speaks out on uncomfortable truths," the jury stated on Friday, explaining its decision to honor Gloger. "Like almost no one else, she has gained access to the very heart of the Kremlin's power elite — from Mikhail Gorbachev to Vladimir Putin.".

According to recent reports, at the prize-giving ceremony, Gloger delivered a passionate plea for more journalism — and more international coverage — in the German press. "We must defend trustworthy, reliable and fact-based journalism with everything in our power," she remarked.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Gloger worked for Reporters Without Borders for 12 years. "The latest rankings show that only one in 100 people can get their information from free, independent journalism and a free, independent press. That shows what's at stake," she said.

The prize winner also mentioned she would dedicate the award to journalists in exile and to her colleagues at Novaya Gazeta, the independent Russian newspaper long known for its critical reporting on the Kremlin. Earlier this week, the paper was forced to shut down its operations in Russia and leave its Moscow newsroom.

In his acceptance speech, Jaafar Abdul Karim said journalism has become more challenging and exhausting than ever. The DW host spoke of hatred and incitement, attacks and threats, both online and offline, in the regions he reports on as well as in Germany.

It has been revealed that such pressure, he remarked, takes a personal toll — yet giving up is not an option. "When I listen to my heart, I know I have to keep going," he said. The answer, he argued, is a form of journalism that fosters dialogue, embraces multiple perspectives and helps bridge divides rather than deepen them.

Recent findings suggest that "I firmly believe in the power of dialogue, today more than ever. That's why we must talk to one another. Even when it gets difficult. Even when we disagree. Or perhaps precisely because of that," he stated.

According to recent reports, listening doesn't mean agreeing, and understanding doesn't mean being in agreement. "Especially now, in times of polarization, when those who believe they're always right are often the loudest, we as journalists have a special responsibility. When everyone is just shouting into their own bubbles or communities, we need journalists who connect these bubbles with one another," he said.

The jury praised Abdul Karim for creating programs at DW that reach millions of young people across the Arab world and in Germany. "His journalism fosters dialogue between countries, between generations, and between religions. He has set latest standards," the jury stated.

According to recent reports, so far in 2026, JaafarTalk has already garnered more than 1.1 billion views across all platforms, and its community has grown to more than 9 million followers. Its motto: "Diversity fosters dialogue.".

"We need fact-based journalism that promotes dialogue and reflects the diversity of our society," Abdul Karim stressed. "By that, I mean an honest and open dialogue in which we do not look away or remain silent. On the contrary, we must take a clear stand against racism, antisemitism, Islamophobia, discrimination, sexism, and hate speech — no matter which side they come from.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The debut of a new Manchester United manager is usually back page news, and it ensures that all eyes will be on whoever is in the dugout when it comes to their first outing.

With that comes major scrutiny and intense pressure, as every result is put under the microscope. For Mauricio Pochettino, the latest United gaffer, an intense 4-0 capitulation at Anfield against bitter long-term rivals Liverpool has meant he has matched the heaviest loss any United manager has suffered in his first game.

A poor start, yes, but he's certainly not alone in the annals of history when it comes to poor United manager debuts: here's the worst five first games for new managers.

Sir Alex Ferguson arrived from Aberdeen after Ron Atkinson's sacking to find a side in the bottom four of the First Division. His first afternoon at the cramped Manor Ground offered no upcoming-manager bounce. John Aldridge's penalty on the stroke of half-time and a late Neil Slatter strike sealed a 2-0 defeat, and United had to wait until a 1-0 win over QPR on 22 November for their first victory under the Scot.

Industry observers note that the rest is history. United recovered to finish 11th, and Ferguson stayed for 26 years as he created one of the greatest managerial dynasties in the sport's history. Winning 13 league titles and two Champions Leagues among a 38-trophy haul. And yet, even one of the greats of the game faced sacking claims.

Scott Duncan's opening day in the Old Trafford dugout ended with Joe Mawson scoring twice as Stoke won 2-0 in the Second Division.

Sources indicate that it foreshadowed a turbulent five years. Despite heavy spending, United came within a whisker of the third tier in 1933/34, surviving only by beating Millwall 2-0 on the final day to send their opponents down instead.

Duncan led United to the Second Division title in 1935/36, but they were relegated straight back down a year later, and he departed for Ipswich Town in November 1937.

John Chapman, appointed from Airdrieonians after Jack Robson stepped down through ill health, watched his fresh side concede five at Old Trafford in his first game.

It set the tone for the campaign as United finished bottom of the First Division and were relegated — one of only four times since their inception in 1878.

Chapman did rebuild, guiding United back to the top flight in 1925, but his reign ended abruptly in October 1926 when the FA suspended him for "improper conduct" – a charge that was never publicly explained.

Chapman's suspension left United without a manager two days before a trip to Burnden Park, and the club handed temporary control to wing-half Lal Hilditch.

The result was a 4-0 thrashing, which stood for a century as the heaviest defeat suffered by a United manager in his first game.

Recent findings suggest that hilditch, the first player-manager in the club's history, was reluctant to pick himself, and the side suffered. He won only nine of his 30 games before Herbert Bamlett took over in April 1927.

Pochettino became the first United boss to begin his reign against Liverpool, and the afternoon unravelled almost immediately.

Leny Yoro was sent off in the eighth minute for a last-man foul on Alexander Isak, the earliest red card shown to a United player in Premier League history. Dominik Szoboszlai scored from the resulting free-kick, and Florian Wirtz doubled the lead within three minutes.

Rio Ngumoha, who became the youngest scorer in the fixture's history, and substitute Víctor Muñoz completed the rout after the break.

Recent findings suggest that pochettino inherited a side that had won once in 10 league games under Michael Carrick, who had guided them to third the season before. The defeat left United 19th in the Premier League table with eight points from 11 games, their lowest tally at that stage of a season since 1972/73.

The post-Ferguson era has produced false dawns in both directions. Many have tried and failed to bring sustained success to the club in what has been a faltering 13 years since Ferguson departed.

Industry observers note that louis van Gaal lost 2-1 at home to Swansea City in 2014, United's first opening-day home defeat since 1972. Erik ten Hag went one worse, losing 2-1 at home to Brighton before a 4-0 hammering at Brentford made him the first United manager in more than a century to lose his first two games. He still went on to win the League Cup and the FA Cup.

Industry observers note that at the other end of the scale, Ole Gunnar Solskjaer's 5-1 win at Cardiff City and David Moyes's 4-1 victory at Swansea in his first league game both preceded reigns that ended in the sack. Ruben Amorim, meanwhile, opened with a 1-1 draw at Ipswich Town and endured a torrid time.

If United's history proves anything, it is that a first result claims little about what follows. Ferguson lost his opening game and built a dynasty. Pochettino now needs a recovery of his own to ensure United drag themselves out of a relegation battle, and start to build a team in his image.

Manchester United 1-0 Crystal Palace.

Ipswich Town 1-1 Manchester United.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Atlético Madrid has completed the purchase of half of Atlético Fútbol Club, the Guayaquil side that won Ecuador's Serie B in its first season. The deal gives the Spanish club its first affiliate in South America before the Ecuadorian team steps up to Serie A in 2027.

The announcement went up on the Madrid club’s website at 19:00 on 13 November 2026.

According to recent reports, the move had been signalled earlier in the year. On Friday 20 February 2026, Atlético remarked it would share sporting, institutional and commercial expertise with Atlético FC and might take a stake in the following months, El Comercio reported.

Regarded as Ecuador’s largest non-profit organisation, the Junta de Beneficencia de Guayaquil operates in all 24 of the country’s provinces.

It has been revealed that the club’s route into Serie B was unusual. It took over the place of Atlético Vinotinto, which could not use it because its affiliate Vinotinto FC had been relegated. The team also changed its name from Atlético JBG to Atlético FC.

Promotion came on 15 October 2026 with a 1-0 win over Independiente Juniors. Fidel Martínez scored the goal. A week later, on Thursday 22 October, a 2-2 draw against Cuenca Juniors at the Estadio Alejandro Serrano sealed the title. That match was the ninth round of the promotion hexagonal.

Across the campaign the side scored 39 goals and conceded 21. It became the 37th different club to win Ecuador’s Serie B. The team is coached by Carlos Santamarina, who comes from Atlético’s academy.

Sources indicate that the promotion also reshapes the city’s football map. Guayaquil will have four clubs in the 2027 Serie A: Atlético FC, Barcelona SC, Emelec and Guayaquil City.

Mexico and Canada already host clubs in the Madrid side’s network of linked teams, through Atlético de San Luis and Atlético Ottawa.

It has been revealed that the investment builds on years of groundwork in Ecuador. Atlético and the Junta signed their original strategic agreement on Monday 24 July 2023 at the charity’s sports complex. Under that deal, the club’s academy would apply its coaching model to the Junta’s football division. At the time, that division served 2,500 children from vulnerable backgrounds.

It has been revealed that in June 2026 the club put the number of young players at more than 14,000. That same month, chief executive Miguel Ángel Gil Marín visited the academy’s Guayaquil base. With the Junta’s delegation, he watched an Atlético FC match and greeted Santamarina.

El Atlético Fútbol Club se une a la familia rojiblanca.

Nuestro club hace efectiva la adquisición del 50% del equipo ecuatoriano, que logró el ascenso a la Serie A en octubre de la mano del técnico de la Academia Carlos Santamarina.

¡Bienvenidos, @AtleticoFCec! ❤️🤍.

— Atlético de Madrid (@Atleti) November 13, 2026.

For Atlético, the stake creates a direct link between that youth work and a senior professional team.

According to recent reports, the board holds its first meeting next week. It will elect a president proposed by Atlético and appoint a general manager.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Manchester City's poor Premier League form continued on Saturday as Enzo Maresca's side made it four games without a win with a 1-1 draw against Fulham.

But the match was not without its controversy.

Rodrigo Muniz put the visitors in front in the 16th minute, but just under ten minutes later, City thought they had levelled the game when Erling Haaland, one of the best strikers in the Premier League right now, prodded through Bernd Leno's legs.

However, the goal was not given on the field of play, with referee Thomas Bramall adjudging Haaland to have fouled the Whites goalkeeper. Elliot Anderson did volley home an equaliser in the second half, but the home side could not force a winner.

That Haaland non-goal left manager Enzo Maresca questioning the officials afterwards.

The City boss said: "I reviewed the goal after the game. From my point of view, it’s quite clear that it’s not a foul, but I’m not the guy that decides, unfortunately.”.

Pundits have been split on the decision, with some suggesting it should have stood, and others agreeing with Bramall and VAR Sam Barrott.

GIVEMESPORT's resident referee expert Graham Barber has now delivered his verdict on the incident.

Speaking exclusively to GMS, he stated: "So, for me, on this one, I'm going to join the goalkeepers' union. Some people say the referees' union and the goalkeepers' union are as one!

It has been revealed that "When I saw it for the first time, I actually thought it was a foul, but when I saw it the second time, he [Leno] actually did lose the ball. But the challenge from Haaland came when the goalkeeper had two hands on the ball.

"And it's very, very difficult to argue a goalkeeper is not in control of the ball, if he's got two hands on the ball, I mean, if he's not got two hands on the ball, you could argue he has to be in control of the ball.

"I found it quite interesting as well that he then fell over into the back of the net and then pulled the ball forward to try and pretend that it didn't go over the goal line, which, considering the technology is in the ball and it's going to be on the referee's watch whether it cross the line is irrelevant.

"For me, the correct decision, Haaland definitely made the challenge, definitely touched the ball while two hands were on the ball, so for me, correct decision.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By ISABEL BALDWIN, US ASSISTANT SPORTS EDITOR.

Published: 10:23 EST, 23 November 2026 | Updated: 11:36 EST, 23 November 2026.

The World Cup is set to return to America after FIFA awarded the 2031 women's tournament to a historic four-nation bid.

Following the success of the men's tournament this summer, the United States was unveiled as one of the hosts of the women's edition in five years' time during a virtual meeting of FIFA's national associations on Monday.

The US will co-host the global soccer extravaganza alongside Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica after the four countries' joint bid was awarded uncontested the 2031 tournament.

The selection marks a milestone for the Women's World Cup with the tournament being hosted across four nations for the first time in its history.

The last World Cup was co-hosted by multiple countries for the first time with the 2023 edition taking place across Australia and Newly introduced Zealand.

This summer's men's World Cup was also co-hosted by the US with games taking place across the States, Canada and Mexico.

The World Cup is set to return to the United States for the 2031 women's edition of the event.

Spain are reigning champions after winning the Women's World Cup in 2023.

The United States Women's National Team are four-time winners in 1991, 1999, 2015 and 2019.

The 2031 tournament will also be the largest in the competition's history, featuring an expanded 48-team field and 104 matches for the first time.

'We are incredibly honored and excited to welcome the world to the United States, Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica for the 2031 FIFA Women's World Cup,' said US Soccer President Cindy Parlow Cone.

According to recent reports, 'This is a historic moment for our four countries, but the opportunity is much bigger than any one of us. Together with FIFA, we want to deliver the biggest and most impactful Women's World Cup in history and use its success to accelerate the growth of women's soccer around the world. Our ambition is to create a tournament that not only inspires millions of players, but helps give them the opportunities to play, grow and pursue their dreams.'.

The selection marks the third time that the Women's World Cup has been awarded to the US with the country previously hosting the landmark 1999 and 2003 editions alone. The national team's tournament win in 1999 was the second of its four titles.

Meanwhile, Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica will become first-time hosts at the historic tournament.

'This milestone furthers the continued belief that the best days of soccer in America are still ahead,' said U.S. Soccer CEO and General Secretary JT Batson.

'We have an opportunity to use the momentum from the 2031 FIFA Women's World Cup to accelerate our ambitions for the future of soccer, from expanding access and participation to strengthening the pathways that develop the next generation of players. We are excited to work alongside our partners across the region to make this tournament a defining moment for women's soccer.'.

The U.S.-led 2031 project across the CONCACAF regional soccer body bid offers FIFA a choice of stadiums in 20 cities: 14 in the U.S., four in Mexico plus San José in Costa Rica and Kingston, Jamaica.

US Soccer President Cindy Parlow Cone said the federation was honored to be selected.

The host selection of the 2035 Women's World Cup was awarded to a joint bid between England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales.

The host selection of the 2035 Women's World Cup was also unveiled on Monday with the tournament being awarded to another joint bid between England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales.

It marks the first time that a World Cup has been hosted on the British Isles since the men's tournament in 1966 in England.

The United Kingdom bid joins England with Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales that offers a choice from 19 venues, including Wembley Stadium in London.

The winning candidates and FIFA president Gianni Infantino promised commercially successful tournaments - the first editions with 48 teams and 104 games - and to reinvest all that money in women's soccer.

FIFA wanted these heavyweights of women's soccer to face no opposition without rival bids and so lead hosting the first expanded tournaments. That will bring parity with the men's World Cup which expanded to 48 teams this year in the US, Canada and Mexico.

The 2027 Women's World Cup will have 32 teams in Brazil.

Aston Villa goalkeeper Zion Suzuki went from being serenaded with a chorus of “world’s No 1” to making a bizarre blunder that denied Unai Emery’s side a third successive Premier League victory.

The Villa manager, however, preferred to focus on a string of crucial saves from Suzuki rather than the uncharacteristic mistake that allowed Fulham to collect a deserved point.

It all went wrong for the hosts just after the hour mark in a match where Fulham provided more than a few scares before finding the net in unexpected fashion.

Alex Iwobi, who had been denied superbly by a Suzuki save just moments earlier, swung in a corner. It was right on top of the Villa goalkeeper, who tried to keep it out but only succeeded in fumbling it over the line. A frantic attempt to gather the ball was in vain and goal-line technology confirmed the goal stood.

Industry observers note that zion Suzuki drops Alex Iwobi's corner and Fulham are level! 🫨 https://t.co/KwLFMRpKqk.

Suzuki appeared to have been put off by the presence of Fulham’s Shea Charles, but Emery refused to single out the player for criticism.

It has been revealed that “I prefer to speak about the saves that he made,” the Villa manager said. “This is part of football. I think he played fantastically and he is doing a lot of saves so he can make one mistake. It is part of football. We can be mature about this.

Industry observers note that “I still want to see consistency. Over the last five Premier League matches, we are winning three and drawing two. It’s not bad but with our poor start it’s not enough.

“We have to change our mind quickly for Tuesday against Barcelona. We want to test ourselves at this level.”.

Villa go to the Nou Camp with a 100 per cent Champions League record to their name this season. But they will need to improve on Saturday evening’s performance to get a result in Spain.

As well as Suzuki’s error, a 14th-minute penalty miss from John McGinn also proved costly.

It was awarded after Leon Goretzka, making his full league debut for Villa, saw his header hit Sander Berge’s raised hand. Nobody appealed at the time but referee Sam Barrott was sent to the touchline monitor by VAR to review the incident and gave the spot-kick.

In a recent development, mcGinn’s attempt, however, hit the crossbar and the chance to take an early lead went begging. The Villa captain seemed a strange choice to take the spot-kick as he has only ever scored one career penalty, but Emery defended the choice, saying: “We analysed the penalty takers in the squad and it was McGinn here.”.
